title: KungfuBot / PBHC: Repair the Motion, Then Tighten Tracking Tolerance
content_lines: Sources: [arXiv:2506.12851](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12851) · [pinned official code](https://github.com/TeleHuman/PBHC/tree/ffac5cded61fe78b39b051f09ac2ed0f6a1ccea0)
Review scope: all twenty-eight pages and appendices, reward/randomization/data specifications, and official filtering, retargeting, adaptive reward, and deployment code.

> In one sentence: PBHC extracts GVHMR motion, filters it with CoM/CoP physics, estimates contact, repairs ground height, retargets by IK, and trains one policy per motion while monotonically shrinking reward tolerance toward an error EMA; G1 demonstrations are broad, but only Tai Chi has ten quantitative trials, and the method lacks environment awareness and a unified multi-skill policy.

Key terms include Physics-Based Humanoid Control (PBHC, 物理人形控制), Human Motion Recovery (HMR, 人体动作恢复), Center of Mass/Pressure (CoM/CoP, 质心/压力中心), contact mask (接触掩码), differential inverse kinematics (微分逆运动学), tracking factor (跟踪因子), bi-level optimization (双层优化), Exponential Moving Average (EMA, 指数移动平均), and asymmetric actor–critic (非对称 actor–critic).
## Engineering problem

Dynamic video motion contains HMR drift, floating feet, and human joint or speed demands a robot cannot realize. With a small exponential-reward tolerance, initial error produces near-zero reward and no useful gradient; with a large tolerance, tracking stays inaccurate. One fixed value cannot fit Tai Chi, jump kicks, and full spins.

Motion processing resembles checking whether a score is playable by an instrument: remove notes outside its range, repair timing and contact, then practice. Adaptive tolerance resembles a coach who first accepts a broad target and tightens it as the athlete improves. Competition tolerance on day one may provide no learning signal.
## Method

The pipeline runs monocular GVHMR, CoM/CoP stability filtering, contact estimation, vertical ground correction plus EMA smoothing, and G1 IK retargeting, with added AMASS/LAFAN data. Of ten test sequences, six accepted motions reach high episode-length ratios, while the four rejected motions reach at most 54%, suggesting the filter removes expensive failures.

Tracking reward is exp(−x/sigma). A simplified bi-level derivation gives an optimum equal to converged average error. Since that value is unknown, PBHC estimates error online and updates sigma to min(sigma, EMA). Monotonic tightening prevents temporary policy deterioration from relaxing the target.
### Input → processing → output

G1 controls twenty-three DoF through PD targets. The actor sees five-step proprioceptive history and motion phase; the critic also receives reference positions, root linear velocity, and randomized physics. Reward vectorization gives each reward its own value head before combining advantages. One PPO policy is trained per reference motion with three seeds and evaluated over 1,000 rollouts.

Sim-to-real uses domain randomization and MuJoCo validation without hardware fine-tuning. Motions are grouped as easy, medium, and hard. The appendix exposes contact, reward, randomization, PD, and adaptive-sigma values, enabling direct configuration audit.

Table 2 uses ten Tai Chi trials and finds onboard body/joint/velocity errors close to MuJoCo. Figure 9 shows convergence near 20k steps. Other dynamic motions do not receive equivalent repeated statistics.
## Decisive evidence

The strongest evidence combines fixed-tolerance ablation with difficulty-stratified Table 1. It directly tests the claimed mechanism rather than attributing gains to more data or a larger model. Three seeds and 1,000 rollouts expose the large hard-motion variance.

The ten-trial Tai Chi sim-real comparison is the strongest hardware quantity, but real root position is unavailable and fixed to the origin. Tai Chi is not the most aggressive jump or spin, so high-dynamic deployment remains mainly qualitative.
## Paper-to-implementation mapping

At commit `ffac5cded61fe78b39b051f09ac2ed0f6a1ccea0`, `smpl_retarget/motion_filter/utils/motion_filter.py::MotionFilter` implements physical filtering, `convert_fit_motion.py::correct_motion` performs contact-aware height repair, and `mink_retarget.py::retarget_fit_motion` maps motion to G1.

`humanoidverse/envs/motion_tracking/general_tracking.py::_update_adaptive_sigma` performs monotonic updates. `_reward_teleop_joint_position` and `_reward_teleop_body_position_extend` feed errors into adaptive tracking. The repository includes broad HumanoidVerse machinery, so exact PBHC configurations must remain pinned.
## Limits and evidence boundary

The authors explicitly state that PBHC lacks terrain perception and obstacle avoidance, and that one policy imitates only one motion. Efficient high-dynamic multi-skill generalization is left to future work.

Independent limitations include a CoM/CoP filter that may reject feasible dynamic flight, only ten filtering examples, cascading HMR/contact/IK/RL errors, unavailable hardware root position, repeated statistics only for Tai Chi, and storage, switching, and audit cost for one policy per motion.

Kicks, spins, and jumps need independent self-collision, slip, landing, torque, speed, power, and workspace guards. Adaptive tolerance improves tracking reward but cannot make an unsafe reference safe. Filtering is not a replacement for actuator and collision envelopes. Use restraint, padding, emergency stop, and per-motion approval.
## Bounded engineering takeaway

The reusable contribution is two feedback loops: audit motion feasibility before training, then tighten reward tolerance as achievable error falls. Inspect filtering and retargeting artifacts before changing PPO.

Single-motion policies make strong research baselines. A future unified controller should be regressed against them per motion on tracking, energy, and hardware gates, making generalization cost explicit.
## Reproduction checklist

Pin PDF, commit, GVHMR, SMPL, datasets, G1 model, contact and CoM/CoP thresholds, EMA, sigma range, PPO, PD, randomization, seeds, and motion list. Reproduce Figure 6–9, Table 1–2, and appendix Table 10–13.

Hash original video, HMR, masks, corrected motion, and retargeted output. Report accepted/rejected ELR. Ablate four fixed tolerances, adaptive tolerance, correction, and masks, with quantiles and hard-motion failure labels.

Stage hardware from Tai Chi and punches to kicks, spins, and jumps. Repeat each and log fall, partial, slip, collision, torque/current, landing impulse, and intervention. Switch only from a verified stable state and reject unknown references or obstructed environments.
> **Engineering judgment:** prove the reference is physically usable before tightening tracking; a polished dynamic video replaces neither motion-data audit nor repeated safety evidence.
